microvilli of isolated brush borders vesiculate in the presence of millimolar Ca(++), that Ca(++), in the absence of ATP, causes the cores to disintegrate, and that the terminal web region remains intact in the presence of ATP or Ca(++).
Ca(++) causes the complete solaton of the core filaments of microvilli and the complete vesiculation (not retraction) of the microvilli.

In summary, our research is concerned with
the motility of the brush border of the enterocyte and the role of Ca(++) in this motility.
the role of Ca(++) in the regulation of brush border cell motility.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the microvilli of isolated intestinal cells do not contract in response to Ca(++), ATP, or to a combination of these agents, but rather, the microvillous cores disintegrate and the membrane vesiculates in response to these agents.
Ca(++), in the absence of ATP, induces the disintegration of the microvillus core filaments.
Ca(++) causes the disintegration of microvillar actin filaments into short actin fragments and the vesiculation of microvilli.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
brush borders are motile, but the motility is a result of Ca(++)/Ca(++)-dependent actin filament solation and membrane vesiculation.
brush border microvillar actin filaments do not retract in response to Ca(++), ATP, or Ca(++), ATP; rather they disintegrate in response to Ca(+).
Ca(++) causes the solation of the actin filaments in microvillar rootlets and cores, but not the terminal web, and that Ca(++) induces vesiculation of microvillar membranes.
The main takeaway from our work is that
Ca(++)-induced core disintegration is not the same as core retraction.
the Ca(++)-induced contraction of microvilli into the terminal web is not a motility mechanism.
the brush border is not motile in response to Ca(++).
